_link.title: I can apply ΔE = Δmc² to calculate energy released in positron–electron annihilation

toLevel2.question: What happens when a positron and an electron meet?
toLevel2.correct: They annihilate, converting all their rest mass into energy
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A positron is the antimatter counterpart of the electron. When they meet, both particles are destroyed and their combined rest mass is converted entirely to energy.

distractors.answer: They repel each other because they have the same mass
distractors.explanation: A positron has positive charge and an electron has negative charge; they attract each other and annihilate.

distractors.answer: They combine to form a neutron with no energy released
distractors.explanation: A neutron is not formed from positron–electron annihilation; the particles convert entirely into gamma-ray photons.

distractors.answer: They orbit each other indefinitely at a fixed distance
distractors.explanation: The positron and electron attract and annihilate almost immediately upon meeting; they do not orbit indefinitely.

toLevel2.question: How many gamma-ray photons are typically produced in positron–electron annihilation?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Two photons are emitted in opposite directions to conserve both energy and momentum in the annihilation event.

distractors.explanation: A single photon cannot conserve momentum; two photons emitted in opposite directions are needed.
While three-photon annihilation is possible in rare cases, the standard annihilation produces exactly two photons.

distractors.answer: No photons are produced in the annihilation
distractors.explanation: The rest mass energy must be carried away by photons; two gamma rays are the standard products of annihilation.

toLevel2.question: What is the rest mass of an electron (and a positron)?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Both the electron and positron have the same rest mass of 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg. The positron has positive charge while the electron has negative charge.

distractors.explanation: This is the mass of a proton, which is approximately 1836 times heavier than an electron.
This is 1000 times too large; the electron mass is 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, not 10⁻²⁷ kg.
This is 1000 times too small; the electron mass is 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, not 10⁻³⁴ kg.

toLevel2.question: In what directions are the two gamma-ray photons emitted during positron–electron annihilation?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The two photons are emitted in opposite directions to conserve momentum, since the initial momentum of the system is approximately zero.

distractors.answer: In the same direction as each other
distractors.explanation: If both photons travelled in the same direction, momentum would not be conserved; they must travel in opposite directions.

distractors.answer: At right angles to each other (90° apart)
distractors.explanation: Momentum conservation requires the photons to be emitted at 180°, not 90°, when the particles are nearly at rest.

distractors.answer: In random directions that change each time
distractors.explanation: The photons are always emitted at 180° to each other to satisfy conservation of momentum.

toLevel2.question: Which medical imaging technique relies on positron–electron annihilation?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: PET scans detect the two gamma-ray photons produced when a positron from a radioactive tracer annihilates with an electron in body tissue.

distractors.explanation: MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves to image tissue; it does not involve positron–electron annihilation.

distractors.answer: X-ray imaging of bones and organs
distractors.explanation: X-rays are produced by electron deceleration in a tube, not by positron–electron annihilation.
Ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves, not gamma rays from annihilation.

toLevel2.question: In positron–electron annihilation, the entire rest mass of both particles is converted to energy.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Both the positron and electron are completely destroyed, and their combined rest mass is converted entirely into the energy of the two gamma-ray photons.

distractors.explanation: Annihilation is a complete conversion of matter and antimatter to energy; no residual massive particles remain.

toLevel2.question: Each gamma-ray photon produced in positron–electron annihilation carries energy equal to the combined rest energy of both particles.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Each photon carries energy equal to the rest energy of one electron (or positron): E = mc² = 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ J. The total energy is split equally between the two photons.

distractors.explanation: The total energy is shared between two photons; each photon carries half the total, which equals the rest energy of one particle.

toLevel2.prompt: Complete the sentence about positron–electron annihilation.
toLevel2.sentence: When a positron meets an electron, they {{blank:1}}, producing two {{blank:2}} that travel in opposite directions.

1.correctExplanation: Annihilation is the complete destruction of a particle and its antiparticle, converting all rest mass to energy.

distractors.explanation: A neutron is not formed; both particles are completely destroyed and their mass becomes gamma-ray energy.
The positron (positive charge) and electron (negative charge) attract and annihilate, they do not repel.

2.correctExplanation: The energy from annihilation appears as two high-energy gamma-ray photons, each with energy equal to the rest energy of one electron.

distractors.explanation: The photons have energy of 0.511 MeV each, which is in the gamma-ray range, far higher than visible light.
Neutrinos are not produced in standard positron–electron annihilation; the products are gamma-ray photons.

toLevel2.prompt: Complete the sentence about annihilation and conservation.
toLevel2.sentence: Two photons are produced in annihilation rather than one because {{blank:1}} must be conserved.

1.correctExplanation: A single photon cannot conserve both energy and momentum simultaneously. Two photons in opposite directions ensure momentum sums to zero.

distractors.explanation: Charge is conserved because both photons are neutral, but this does not explain why two photons are needed instead of one.
Rest mass is not conserved in annihilation; the requirement for two photons comes from momentum conservation.

toLevel2.prompt: Complete the sentence about PET scans.
toLevel2.sentence: PET scans work by detecting the two {{blank:1}} produced when a positron from a radioactive tracer annihilates with an {{blank:2}} in the patient's body.

1.correctExplanation: The two 0.511 MeV gamma-ray photons travel in opposite directions and are detected by sensors around the patient.

distractors.explanation: The photons produced in annihilation have energy of 0.511 MeV, which is in the gamma-ray range, not the X-ray range.
Alpha particles are helium nuclei; annihilation produces gamma-ray photons, not alpha particles.

2.correctExplanation: The positron from the tracer annihilates with an electron in the surrounding tissue, producing two gamma rays.

distractors.explanation: Positron–proton annihilation does not occur; positrons annihilate with their antiparticle, the electron.
Positrons do not annihilate with neutrons; they annihilate with electrons, which are their antimatter counterpart.

toLevel3.question: Calculate the rest energy of a single electron using E = mc².

distractors.explanation: This results from multiplying by c instead of c²; the formula requires the speed of light to be squared.
This fails to multiply by c² at all; the rest mass alone is not the rest energy.
This results from dividing by c² instead of multiplying; the rest energy is much larger than the mass value.

toLevel3.question: Explain why the total energy released in positron–electron annihilation is 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ J, not 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ J.
toLevel3.correct: Because both particles contribute their rest mass energy: 2 × 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ = 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ J
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Both the electron and positron have rest energy mc² = 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ J. The total energy released is the sum of both rest energies.

distractors.answer: Because the gamma-ray photons gain extra energy from the electromagnetic field during annihilation
distractors.explanation: The total energy comes from the rest mass of both particles; no additional energy is gained from external fields.

distractors.answer: Because the positron has twice the mass of the electron at the point of annihilation
distractors.explanation: The positron and electron have identical masses; the total is doubled because there are two particles.

distractors.answer: Because kinetic energy of the particles before annihilation doubles the rest energy released
distractors.explanation: The 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ J accounts for both rest masses; if the particles had kinetic energy, the total would exceed this value.

toLevel3.question: What is the energy of each gamma-ray photon produced in positron–electron annihilation, expressed in MeV?
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Each photon carries the rest energy of one electron: 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ J = 0.511 MeV. This is a well-known value in particle physics.

distractors.explanation: 1.022 MeV is the total energy released from both particles; each individual photon carries half this amount.
This would imply the energy is split four ways; in standard annihilation, two photons share the total energy equally.
931.5 MeV is the energy equivalent of 1 atomic mass unit; the electron rest energy is much smaller at 0.511 MeV.

toLevel3.question: Explain why positron–electron annihilation is described as a complete conversion of mass to energy, unlike nuclear fusion.
toLevel3.correct: In annihilation, all rest mass of both particles is converted to photon energy, whereas in fusion only a small mass defect is converted
toLevel3.correctExplanation: In fusion, the products retain most of their mass. In annihilation, no massive particles remain — the entire rest mass becomes photon energy.

distractors.answer: In annihilation, energy is produced but the particles are not actually destroyed
distractors.explanation: The particles are completely destroyed; no electron or positron remains after annihilation.

distractors.answer: In fusion, all the mass is converted but annihilation only converts half the mass
distractors.explanation: The opposite is true; annihilation converts all rest mass while fusion converts only a small fraction.

distractors.answer: Both processes convert the same fraction of mass to energy but at different rates
distractors.explanation: Annihilation converts 100% of rest mass; fusion converts a tiny fraction (less than 1%).

toLevel3.question: Why must the two gamma-ray photons from positron–electron annihilation have equal energy when the particles are at rest?
toLevel3.correct: Equal energies ensure that both energy and momentum are conserved simultaneously
toLevel3.correctExplanation: With zero initial momentum, the photons must have equal and opposite momenta. Since photon momentum is E/c, equal momenta require equal energies.

distractors.answer: Because the electron and positron have equal charge magnitudes that produce equal photon energies
distractors.explanation: Photon energy is determined by conservation of energy and momentum, not by the charges of the annihilating particles.

distractors.answer: Because gamma rays always have the same fixed energy regardless of the process that produces them
distractors.explanation: Gamma-ray energies vary widely; the 0.511 MeV energy is specific to electron–positron annihilation at rest.

distractors.answer: Because photons cannot carry different amounts of energy in the same reaction
distractors.explanation: Photons can have different energies; the equal energies here result from momentum conservation with zero initial momentum.

toLevel3.question: A student claims the total energy from annihilation of a positron and electron at rest is 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ J. Show how this value is obtained.
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The total mass annihilated is 2m = 2 × 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ = 1.822 × 10⁻³⁰ kg. Multiplying by c² gives 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ J.

distractors.answer: ΔE = mc² = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ J for both particles combined
distractors.explanation: This only accounts for one particle; both the positron and electron contribute rest mass, so the factor of 2 is needed.
The formula requires c², not c; multiplying by c alone gives an incorrect and much smaller result.

distractors.answer: ΔE = m²c² = (9.11 × 10⁻³¹)² × (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 7.48 × 10⁻⁴⁵ J for both particles
distractors.explanation: The formula is ΔE = 2mc², not m²c²; squaring the mass is incorrect.

toLevel3.question: If a positron and electron are both moving with significant kinetic energy before annihilation, the total energy of the gamma-ray photons would exceed 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ J.
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The total energy of the photons equals the combined rest energy plus any kinetic energy the particles had before annihilation. Kinetic energy adds to the total.

distractors.explanation: Conservation of energy requires all energy (rest plus kinetic) to appear in the photons; additional kinetic energy increases the total.

toLevel3.prompt: Complete the calculation of total energy released in annihilation.

1.correctExplanation: c² = (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 9.00 × 10¹⁶ m² s⁻². This is the square of the speed of light.

distractors.explanation: This is c, not c²; the mass–energy formula requires the speed of light to be squared.
This is Planck's constant; it is not used in the mass–energy equivalence formula.
This is the rest energy of only one particle; annihilation involves both particles, so the total is doubled.
This fails to multiply by c²; the energy is many orders of magnitude larger than the mass value.

toLevel3.prompt: Complete the sentence about energy per photon in annihilation.
toLevel3.sentence: Each gamma-ray photon from annihilation at rest carries energy {{blank:1}} × 10⁻¹⁴ J, which equals {{blank:2}} MeV.

1.correctExplanation: Each photon carries the rest energy of one electron: mc² = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 9.00 × 10¹⁶ = 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ J.

distractors.explanation: 16.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ J is the total energy from both particles; each photon carries half this amount.
4.10 × 10⁻¹⁴ J would be one quarter of the total energy; each photon carries exactly half.

2.correctExplanation: 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ J = 0.511 MeV. This is the well-known rest energy of the electron in MeV.

distractors.explanation: 1.022 MeV is the total energy from both particles; each photon carries 0.511 MeV.
938.3 MeV is the rest energy of a proton, not an electron; the electron rest energy is 0.511 MeV.

toLevel3.prompt: Complete the sentence about momentum conservation in annihilation.
toLevel3.sentence: The two photons from annihilation travel in {{blank:1}} directions to conserve {{blank:2}}.

1.correctExplanation: When the initial momentum is approximately zero, the two photons must travel in opposite directions so their momenta cancel.

distractors.explanation: If both photons went the same way, momentum would not be conserved; they must go in opposite directions.
Perpendicular emission would not cancel the momenta; opposite directions are required for zero total momentum.

2.correctExplanation: Conservation of momentum requires the total momentum after annihilation to equal the total momentum before. With zero initial momentum, the photon momenta must cancel.

distractors.explanation: Both photons are neutral regardless of direction; the directional requirement comes from momentum conservation.
Rest mass is not conserved in annihilation; the directional constraint arises from momentum conservation.

toLevel4.question: Calculate the total energy released when a positron (mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg) annihilates with an electron (mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg) at rest.

distractors.explanation: This is the rest energy of only one particle; both the positron and electron are annihilated, doubling the energy.
This results from multiplying total mass by c instead of c²; the formula requires c squared.
This results from dividing by c² instead of multiplying; the energy is much larger than the mass.

toLevel4.question: A PET scanner detects two gamma-ray photons from an annihilation event. Each photon has an energy of 0.511 MeV. Convert this energy to joules (1 MeV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J).
toLevel4.correctExplanation: E = 0.511 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ = 8.18 × 10⁻¹⁴ J. This matches mc² for an electron.

distractors.explanation: This converts 0.511 MeV using an incorrect conversion factor; 0.511 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ = 8.18 × 10⁻¹⁴ J.
This is off by one order of magnitude; 0.511 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ gives a result in the 10⁻¹⁴ range.
This incorrectly uses 1 MeV = 10⁻¹³ J without the 1.60 factor; the correct conversion gives 8.18 × 10⁻¹⁴ J.

toLevel4.question: In a PET scan, 2.50 × 10¹⁰ annihilation events occur during the scan. Calculate the total energy released.
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Each event releases 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ J. Total = 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ × 2.50 × 10¹⁰ = 4.10 × 10⁻³ J.

distractors.explanation: This uses the energy per photon rather than per annihilation event; each event produces 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ J total.
This represents the energy from a single event multiplied by about 2.5; the correct calculation uses 2.50 × 10¹⁰ events.
This is off by six orders of magnitude; each event releases only 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ J, so the total is in the millijoule range.

toLevel4.question: A positron with kinetic energy 3.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ J annihilates with a stationary electron. What is the total energy of the two gamma-ray photons produced?
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Total = rest energy of both particles + kinetic energy of positron = 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ + 3.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ = 1.94 × 10⁻¹³ J.

distractors.explanation: This is only the combined rest energy; the kinetic energy of the positron must also be included in the total.
This incorrectly uses only one particle's rest energy plus the kinetic energy; both rest energies contribute.
This is only the kinetic energy of the positron; the rest energy of both particles must also be included.

toLevel4.question: Priya detects gamma rays with energy 0.511 MeV each arriving at two detectors on opposite sides of a patient simultaneously. Calculate the total rest mass annihilated.

distractors.explanation: This is the mass of only one particle; both the positron and electron were annihilated.
This is 1000 times too large; the combined mass of an electron and positron is 1.82 × 10⁻³⁰ kg.
This results from dividing by c⁴ instead of c²; the correct formula is m = E/c².

toLevel4.question: Calculate the frequency of a gamma-ray photon produced in positron–electron annihilation. Use E = hf where h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
toLevel4.correctExplanation: f = E/h = 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ = 1.24 × 10²⁰ Hz. This is in the gamma-ray range.

distractors.explanation: This uses the total energy of both photons; the frequency of each photon is calculated from the energy of one photon.
This has the wrong sign on the exponent; the frequency is a very large number, not a very small one.
This results from multiplying E × h instead of dividing; the correct formula is f = E/h.

toLevel4.question: Arun observes that 5.00 × 10⁸ annihilation events per second occur in a laboratory sample. What power is being produced by annihilation?
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Power = energy per event × events per second = 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ × 5.00 × 10⁸ = 8.20 × 10⁻⁵ W.

distractors.explanation: This uses the energy of one photon per event instead of the total energy per event (1.64 × 10⁻¹³ J).
This fails to multiply by the event rate; power requires energy per second, not energy per event.
This is ten orders of magnitude too large; the energy per event is 10⁻¹³ J, giving power in the 10⁻⁵ W range.

toLevel4.sentence: Total mass annihilated = 2 × {{blank:1}} = 1.822 × 10⁻³⁰ kg. Total energy released = 1.822 × 10⁻³⁰ × 9.00 × 10¹⁶ = {{blank:2}} J.

1.correctExplanation: Each particle (electron and positron) has mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg. The total annihilated mass is twice this.

distractors.explanation: This is the mass of a proton, not an electron; the electron mass is 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
This is already the combined mass of both particles; it should not be doubled again.
This is the energy from one particle only; the total from both is 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ J.
This results from dividing by c² instead of multiplying; the energy is much larger than the mass.

toLevel4.prompt: Complete the calculation involving kinetic energy and annihilation.
toLevel4.sentence: A positron with kinetic energy 5.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ J annihilates with a stationary electron. The total photon energy is {{blank:1}} + {{blank:2}} = 2.14 × 10⁻¹³ J.

1.correctExplanation: The combined rest energy of both particles is 2mc² = 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ J.

distractors.explanation: This is the rest energy of one particle only; both contribute rest energy to the total.
This is the kinetic energy of the positron, not the rest energy of both particles.

2.correctExplanation: The kinetic energy of the positron is added to the combined rest energy: 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ + 5.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ = 2.14 × 10⁻¹³ J.

distractors.explanation: This is the rest energy already accounted for; the second term should be the additional kinetic energy.
This is the rest energy of one particle; the additional term is the positron's kinetic energy of 5.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ J.

toLevel4.prompt: Complete the sentence about the wavelength of annihilation photons.
toLevel4.sentence: Using E = hc/λ, the wavelength of each annihilation photon is λ = hc/E = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸) / 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ = {{blank:1}} m, which is in the {{blank:2}} range of the electromagnetic spectrum.

distractors.explanation: This wavelength is in the infrared range; annihilation photons have a much shorter wavelength in the picometre range.
This wavelength is in the microwave range; gamma-ray photons have wavelengths many orders of magnitude shorter.

2.correctExplanation: A wavelength of 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m (2.43 pm) is in the gamma-ray region of the electromagnetic spectrum.

distractors.explanation: Visible light has wavelengths around 400–700 nm; 2.43 pm is far shorter, in the gamma-ray range.
Ultraviolet radiation has wavelengths around 10–400 nm; 2.43 pm is much shorter, in the gamma-ray range.

toLevel5.question: A student claims that pair production (creating an electron and positron from a photon) requires a minimum photon energy of 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ J. Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.correct: The claim is incorrect; the minimum energy is 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ J because both an electron and a positron must be created
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Pair production creates two particles, so the minimum energy equals the combined rest energy: 2mc² = 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ J (1.022 MeV).

distractors.answer: The claim is correct; only one particle's rest energy is needed because the other is supplied by the nucleus
distractors.explanation: The nucleus provides momentum conservation but not energy; the photon must supply at least 2mc² for both particles.

distractors.answer: The claim is correct; pair production creates only one particle, so only mc² is needed
distractors.explanation: Pair production always creates a particle–antiparticle pair; both masses must be accounted for in the energy threshold.

distractors.answer: The claim is incorrect; pair production requires 3mc² because the photon must also conserve momentum
distractors.explanation: The threshold energy in the presence of a nucleus is 2mc²; the nucleus absorbs recoil momentum without needing additional photon energy.

toLevel5.question: Evaluate why a single photon cannot spontaneously convert into an electron–positron pair in empty space, even if the photon has sufficient energy.
toLevel5.correct: A single photon in empty space cannot simultaneously conserve both energy and momentum during pair production
toLevel5.correctExplanation: In the centre-of-momentum frame of the pair, the initial photon would need zero momentum, but photons always travel at c. A nearby nucleus is needed to absorb the excess momentum.

distractors.answer: A single photon does not have enough energy for pair production under any circumstances
distractors.explanation: A photon with energy ≥ 1.022 MeV has sufficient energy; the issue is momentum conservation, not energy.

distractors.answer: Pair production requires two photons to collide because a single photon cannot create charged particles
distractors.explanation: While two-photon pair production is possible, the issue with one photon is momentum conservation, not charge creation.

distractors.answer: Photons are massless and therefore cannot create particles with mass regardless of the conditions
distractors.explanation: Photons regularly create massive particles in pair production; the constraint in empty space is momentum conservation.

toLevel5.question: Mei argues that annihilation violates conservation of charge because two charged particles become two neutral photons. Evaluate her reasoning.
toLevel5.correct: Charge is conserved because the positron has +e and the electron has −e, giving a total charge of zero before and after
toLevel5.correctExplanation: The initial total charge is (+e) + (−e) = 0. The two photons are neutral, so the final total charge is also 0. Charge is conserved.

distractors.answer: Her reasoning is correct; annihilation does violate charge conservation
distractors.explanation: Charge is always conserved in every physical process; the initial total charge of the system is zero.

distractors.answer: Charge is not conserved, but this is allowed in quantum electrodynamics at high energies
distractors.explanation: Charge conservation is absolute in quantum electrodynamics and is never violated, regardless of energy.

distractors.answer: Charge is conserved because each photon carries one unit of positive and one unit of negative charge
distractors.explanation: Photons are electrically neutral and carry no charge; charge conservation holds because the initial total charge is zero.

toLevel5.question: A PET scanner detects two 0.511 MeV photons arriving at detectors 0.80 m apart. The photons arrive within 2.0 ns of each other. Evaluate whether this event is consistent with a genuine annihilation.
toLevel5.correct: This is consistent; the small time difference indicates the annihilation occurred slightly off-centre, which is expected for events inside a patient
toLevel5.correctExplanation: A 2.0 ns time difference corresponds to a position offset of about 0.30 m from the midpoint. This is within the patient's body and is a normal PET measurement.

distractors.answer: This cannot be an annihilation because both photons should arrive at exactly the same time
distractors.explanation: Simultaneous arrival only occurs if the event is at the exact midpoint; off-centre events produce measurable time differences.

distractors.answer: This is not consistent because the time difference is too large for photons travelling at the speed of light
distractors.explanation: At c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, a 2.0 ns difference corresponds to 0.60 m path difference, which is reasonable for an 0.80 m detector pair.

distractors.answer: This cannot be a genuine annihilation because PET photons are always detected simultaneously
distractors.explanation: PET scanners specifically measure the time difference between photon arrivals to determine the location of the annihilation event.

toLevel5.question: Evaluate the claim: 'Annihilation is the reverse of pair production, so the two processes must release and absorb exactly the same amount of energy.'
toLevel5.correct: This is true for particles at rest; annihilation at rest releases 1.022 MeV and pair production requires at least 1.022 MeV of photon energy
toLevel5.correctExplanation: At rest, the minimum energy threshold for both processes is 2mc² = 1.022 MeV. Additional kinetic energy would alter the total but the rest-energy threshold is symmetric.

distractors.answer: The claim is false; pair production always requires more energy than annihilation releases due to recoil losses
distractors.explanation: The energy threshold for pair production near a nucleus is 2mc², the same as the rest energy released in annihilation at rest.

distractors.answer: The claim is true; both processes always involve exactly 0.511 MeV regardless of particle kinetic energy
distractors.explanation: 0.511 MeV is the energy per photon for annihilation at rest; if particles have kinetic energy, the total changes.

distractors.answer: The claim is false; annihilation releases more energy because it converts two particles while pair production creates only one
distractors.explanation: Pair production creates both an electron and a positron; the minimum energy threshold equals the energy released in annihilation at rest.

toLevel5.question: Sofia claims that annihilation proves Einstein's E = mc² because mass literally becomes light energy. Evaluate the accuracy of this statement.
toLevel5.correct: The statement is essentially correct; annihilation is one of the clearest demonstrations of mass–energy equivalence, with all rest mass becoming photon energy
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Annihilation converts 100% of the rest mass of both particles into photon energy, providing direct and complete experimental confirmation of E = mc².

distractors.answer: The statement is incorrect; E = mc² only applies to nuclear reactions, not particle annihilation
distractors.explanation: E = mc² applies universally to all mass–energy conversions, including annihilation, fusion, and fission.

distractors.answer: The statement is incorrect; the mass does not become energy but rather changes form into something else entirely
distractors.explanation: The mass is genuinely converted to energy in the form of photons; this is exactly what E = mc² describes.

distractors.answer: The statement is misleading; annihilation only confirms conservation of charge, not mass–energy equivalence
distractors.explanation: Charge conservation is also confirmed, but the primary significance is the complete conversion of mass to energy.

toLevel5.question: A textbook states that 'a positron is an electron with positive charge.' Evaluate the completeness of this description.
toLevel5.correct: The description is incomplete; a positron has the same mass and spin as an electron but opposite charge and is classified as antimatter
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Describing the positron as an electron with positive charge captures the charge difference but omits its classification as the antiparticle of the electron, which is physically significant for annihilation.

distractors.answer: The description is fully complete and captures all relevant physical properties of the positron
distractors.explanation: It omits the antimatter nature of the positron, which is essential for understanding why annihilation occurs.

distractors.answer: The description is wrong; a positron has different mass and different spin than an electron
distractors.explanation: A positron has exactly the same mass and spin magnitude as an electron; only the charge sign differs.

distractors.answer: The description is wrong; a positron is actually a proton with reduced mass and increased charge
distractors.explanation: A positron is not related to a proton; it is the antiparticle of the electron with identical mass to the electron.

toLevel5.question: Evaluate whether positron–electron annihilation could be used as a practical energy source.
toLevel5.correct: It is impractical because producing positrons requires more energy than is released by their subsequent annihilation
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Creating a positron (via pair production or beta-plus decay) requires at least as much energy as annihilation releases. There is no net energy gain.

distractors.answer: It is practical because annihilation converts 100% of mass to energy, making it the most efficient process possible
distractors.explanation: While 100% efficient in conversion, the energy cost of producing positrons exceeds the energy recovered from annihilation.

distractors.answer: It is impractical only because positrons decay too quickly to be stored for use as fuel
distractors.explanation: Positrons are stable particles that do not decay; the issue is the energy cost of production, not stability.

distractors.answer: It is practical and is already used in experimental fusion reactors to boost energy output
distractors.explanation: Annihilation is not used in fusion reactors; the energy economics of positron production make it impractical as an energy source.

toLevel5.prompt: Complete the evaluation about pair production and annihilation symmetry.
toLevel5.sentence: Pair production requires a minimum photon energy of {{blank:1}} MeV, which equals the total rest energy of an electron and a positron. This is the {{blank:2}} of annihilation at rest.

1.correctExplanation: The minimum photon energy for pair production is 2 × 0.511 = 1.022 MeV, matching the total rest energy of both particles.

distractors.explanation: 0.511 MeV is the rest energy of one particle only; pair production creates two particles requiring 1.022 MeV minimum.
938.3 MeV is the rest energy of a proton; the electron–positron pair requires 1.022 MeV.

2.correctExplanation: Pair production creates matter from energy, while annihilation converts matter to energy. They are reverse processes with the same energy threshold.

distractors.explanation: Pair production and annihilation are opposite processes, not identical; one creates particles, the other destroys them.
The processes are directly related as time-reversed versions of each other in quantum electrodynamics.

toLevel5.prompt: Complete the evaluation about the practical significance of annihilation in medicine.
toLevel5.sentence: In PET scans, the detection of two {{blank:1}} MeV photons arriving at detectors on opposite sides of the patient confirms that an annihilation event occurred along the line connecting the two {{blank:2}}.

1.correctExplanation: Each gamma-ray photon from annihilation at rest carries 0.511 MeV, which is the signature energy that PET detectors are calibrated to detect.

distractors.explanation: 1.022 MeV is the total energy of both photons; each individual photon carries 0.511 MeV.
This would imply the energy is split four ways; each of the two photons carries exactly 0.511 MeV.

2.correctExplanation: By identifying which two detectors fire simultaneously, the scanner determines the line along which the annihilation occurred, enabling image reconstruction.

distractors.explanation: The detectors detect photons, not electrons; the annihilation location is determined from the detector positions.
The radioactive tracer emits the positron, but the detection line is defined by the two detector positions.
